concepts.title: Tissue Culture, Totipotency and Micro-propagation
concepts.definition: Any living part of a plant excised and grown sterile in a nutrient tube -- an explant -- can regenerate an entire organism, a capacity called totipotency; scaling this up produces thousands of genetically identical somaclones in weeks (micro-propagation), and because apical and axillary meristems always stay virus-free even in sick plants, culturing an excised meristem recovers healthy stock of banana, sugarcane or potato.
concepts.key_idea: The medium must play chemist -- carbon source such as sucrose, inorganic salts, vitamins, amino acids and growth regulators like auxins and cytokinins -- for the explant to rebuild a whole plant.
concepts.textbook_ref: lebo110.txt lines 54-79 (explant, totipotency, nutrient medium, micro-propagation, somaclones, meristem culture)
question_patterns: define totipotency and explain how an explant regrows a whole plant
what does a tissue culture nutrient medium have to supply
why does micropropagation produce genetically identical plants called somaclones
which plant part yields virus free plants and why is it free of virus
how has meristem culture rescued commercially important crops
compare micropropagation with conventional breeding for speed of plant production

solution_steps.explain: Since the 1950s scientists knew whole plants regenerate from any excised part (explant) grown sterile in a special nutrient medium -- every living cell retains the full genetic programme.
The medium supplies a carbon source (sucrose), inorganic salts, vitamins, amino acids and growth regulators such as auxins and cytokinins.
Micro-propagation turns the trick into thousands of plants in short order, each a somaclone identical to the parent -- tomato, banana and apple are done commercially.
Meristems (apical and axillary) escape viral infection even in diseased plants, so excising and culturing them in vitro yields virus-free banana, sugarcane and potato.

concepts.title: Protoplast Fusion and Somatic Hybridisation
concepts.definition: Digesting away the cell walls of single plant cells leaves naked protoplasts wrapped only in plasma membrane; fusing protoplasts from two chosen varieties generates a hybrid protoplast that grows into a somatic hybrid plant carrying traits of both -- the tomato-potato fusion nicknamed pomato worked technically, though the combination never suited commerce.
concepts.key_idea: Strip the walls, merge the membranes -- somatic hybridisation crosses sexual barriers by fusing cells instead of gametes.
concepts.textbook_ref: lebo110.txt lines 80-95 (protoplast isolation, fusion, somatic hybrids, pomato)
question_patterns: what are protoplasts and how are they isolated from plant cells
explain somatic hybridisation with the pomato example
how does protoplast fusion differ from conventional sexual hybridisation
what is a somatic hybrid plant
why did the pomato fail commercially despite the technical success
which enzyme action prepares plant cells for protoplast fusion

solution_steps.explain: Single cells isolated from two varieties are treated to digest their walls, leaving protoplasts enclosed only by plasma membranes.
Protoplasts each carrying a desirable character are fused into hybrid protoplasts.
The fused cell regenerates into a somatic hybrid plant mixing both parents' traits -- tomato plus potato yielded the famous pomato, a laboratory success without commercial payoff.

concepts.title: GM Crops and Their Benefits
concepts.definition: Plants, bacteria, fungi and animals whose genes humans have altered are gene-modified organisms, and gm crops answer the gaps the green revolution left: tolerance to abiotic stresses like cold, drought, salt and heat, less pesticide dependence through pest-resistant varieties, reduced post-harvest losses, more efficient mineral use that spares soil fertility, and better nutrition -- the vitamin a enriched golden rice being the emblem -- plus tailor-made industrial starches, fuels and pharmaceuticals.
concepts.key_idea: Agrochemicals are costly and conventional breeding has plateaued -- gene modification adds traits breeding cannot deliver fast enough.
concepts.textbook_ref: lebo110.txt lines 42-118 (three agriculture options, green revolution limits, five GM benefits, golden rice)
question_patterns: list the benefits genetic modification brings to crop plants
what is golden rice and why was it engineered
why did the green revolution alone fail to secure food supply
compare agrochemical based organic and gene engineered agriculture
how do gm crops reduce reliance on chemical pesticides
which gm trait helps prevent early exhaustion of soil fertility

solution_steps.explain: The green revolution tripled food but mostly via agrochemicals that developing-world farmers cannot afford, and conventional breeding has squeezed out the yield gains it can.
Organisms whose genes people have deliberately altered -- plants, bacteria, fungi, animals -- are gene-modified organisms.
Stress tolerance (cold, drought, salt, heat), built-in pest resistance, lower post-harvest losses, efficient mineral use, and enhanced nutrition as in vitamin a rich golden rice.
Tailor-made plants also supply alternative resources -- starches, fuels and pharmaceuticals -- to industry.

concepts.title: Bt Toxin, cry Genes and Bt Cotton
concepts.definition: Bacillus thuringiensis packs insecticidal protein crystals during one growth phase, but the poison sits as inactive protoxin that only dissolves and activates in an insect's alkaline midgut -- sparing the bacterium itself; the cloned cry genes (cryiac and cryiiab against cotton bollworm, cryiab against corn borer) expressed in plants give built-in protection to bt cotton, corn, rice, tomato, potato and soyabean, killing lepidopterans, coleopterans and dipterans by punching pores in midgut cells that swell and lyse.
concepts.key_idea: Alkaline gut chemistry is the switch -- the protoxin is harmless everywhere until an insect's own digestion arms it.
concepts.textbook_ref: lebo110.txt lines 119-148 (Bt toxin crystals, protoxin activation, cry genes, Bt cotton and crops)
question_patterns: why do bt toxin crystals not kill the bacillus that makes them
how does the inactive protoxin become lethal inside the insect gut
which cry genes protect cotton against bollworms
name the insect groups killed by bt toxin proteins
what is bt cotton and how was the toxin gene introduced
why does the activated toxin cause midgut cells to swell and lyse

solution_steps.explain: Some bacillus thuringiensis strains form protein crystals containing a toxic insecticidal protein during a particular growth phase.
The toxin exists as inactive protoxin; only when an insect ingests it does the alkaline pH of the gut solubilise the crystals and arm the toxin -- which is why the bacterium survives its own poison.
Activated toxin binds midgut epithelial surfaces and opens pores; the cells swell and lyse, and the insect dies -- with specificity per insect group (lepidopterans, coleopterans, dipterans).

Specific cry genes cloned from the bacterium were expressed in crops -- cryiac and cryiiab guard cotton from bollworms, cryiab shields corn from borers -- creating bio-pesticide plants like bt cotton without sprays.

concepts.title: RNA Interference and Nematode-Resistant Tobacco
concepts.definition: Rna interference is a eukaryotic cellular defence that silences a specific mrna when a complementary double-stranded rna binds and blocks its translation; engineers exploited it against the root nematode meloidegyne incognitia by introducing nematode-specific genes through agrobacterium vectors arranged to make both sense and anti-sense rna -- the pair anneals into dsrna, the parasite's mrna falls silent, and the transgenic tobacco roots stay healthy.
concepts.key_idea: Feed the parasite its own mirror -- sense plus antisense transcripts build the dsrna trigger that switches off the nematode's essential genes.
concepts.textbook_ref: lebo110.txt lines 149-167 (Meloidogyne incognitia, RNAi mechanism, sense and anti-sense RNA, protected transgenic host)
question_patterns: explain the mechanism of rna interference as a cellular defence
how was rnai used to protect tobacco plants from nematode infection
which nematode attacks tobacco roots and what damage does it cause
why do sense and antisense rna molecules together stop translation
what role do agrobacterium vectors play in the rnai strategy
name the natural sources of double stranded rna inside cells

solution_steps.explain: Rnai occurs in all eukaryotes: a complementary dsrna molecule binds a specific mrna and prevents its translation -- silencing the gene.
The complementary rna can arise from rna-genomed virus infections or from transposons replicating through an rna intermediate.
Using agrobacterium vectors, nematode-specific genes were installed in the host so its cells transcribe both sense and anti-sense rna, which anneal into dsrna.
The dsrna silences the nematode's own mrna, meloidegyne incognitia cannot survive in the transgenic host, and the tobacco roots escape the yield-robbing infestation.

concepts.title: Genetically Engineered Insulin
concepts.definition: Human insulin is two short polypeptide chains, a and b, joined by disulphide bridges and cut from a longer pro-hormone whose c peptide is discarded during maturation; animal pancreas extracts triggered allergies, so in 1983 eli lilly built dna sequences for the a and b chains into plasmids of e coli, produced the chains separately and joined them with disulphide bonds -- bacterium-made human insulin, identical to the natural hormone.
concepts.key_idea: The c peptide is the assembly headache -- bacteria make the chains, but maturation had to be mimicked by extracting both chains and bridging them chemically.
concepts.textbook_ref: lebo110.txt lines 176-225 (recombinant therapeutics, insulin chains, C peptide, Eli Lilly 1983)
question_patterns: why does insulin from slaughtered animals cause allergic reactions in some patients
describe the structure of mature human insulin and its two chains
what is the c peptide and when is it removed from pro insulin
how did eli lilly produce human insulin in bacteria in 1983
why must insulin be injected rather than swallowed
how many recombinant therapeutics are approved worldwide and how many are marketed in india

solution_steps.explain: Insulin was once extracted from cattle and pig pancreases; being foreign protein, it provoked allergy and other reactions in some patients.
Mature insulin has an a chain and a b chain cross-linked by disulphide bridges; in mammals it is first made as a pro-hormone carrying an extra c peptide that must be excised during maturation.

Eli lilly prepared two dna sequences matching the a and b chains, inserted them into e coli plasmids, grew the chains separately, extracted them and stitched them into mature human insulin via disulphide bonds.
About 30 recombinant therapeutics are approved for humans worldwide and 12 are marketed in india; being identical to human proteins they avoid the unwanted immunological responses of animal extracts.

concepts.title: Gene Therapy: Correcting ADA Deficiency
concepts.definition: Gene therapy is a set of methods for correcting a gene defect diagnosed in a child or embryo by inserting normal genes into the patient's cells and tissues to take over the failed gene's job; the 1990 landmark treated a four-year-old with adenosine deaminase deficiency -- lymphocytes grown outside the body received a functional ada cdna through a retroviral vector and were returned, requiring periodic infusions since such cells are not immortal, while introducing the gene at the embryonic stage could cure permanently.
concepts.key_idea: Lymphocyte therapy buys time, embryonic delivery buys a lifetime -- the difference between periodic infusion and permanent cure.
concepts.textbook_ref: lebo110.txt lines 226-249 (gene therapy definition, 1990 ADA case, retroviral vector, marrow and enzyme replacement options)
question_patterns: what is gene therapy and which defect did the first clinical attempt treat
outline the steps of gene therapy given to the ada deficient girl
why does ada deficiency damage the immune system
compare bone marrow transplantation with enzyme replacement therapy for ada deficiency
why must genetically engineered lymphocytes be re infused periodically
how could introducing ada cdna at the embryonic stage give a permanent cure

solution_steps.explain: Gene therapy inserts genes into a person's cells and tissues so a normal copy compensates for the non-functional one -- the first clinical application came in 1990.
Deletion of the adenosine deaminase gene cripples the immune system; marrow transplantation or injected functional ada help some children but neither cures completely.

The patient's blood lymphocytes are cultured outside the body, a functional ada cdna is delivered by a retroviral vector, and the engineered cells are returned -- repeated because lymphocytes die off.
Introducing the ada gene isolated from marrow-producing cells into cells at early embryonic stages could fix the defect for life.

concepts.title: Molecular Diagnosis: PCR, Probes and ELISA
concepts.definition: Conventional serum and urine analysis cannot catch a disease early, but molecular tools can: pcr amplifies vanishingly small amounts of pathogen nucleic acid before symptoms show (routine for hiv and for mutations in suspected cancers), a radiolabelled single-stranded dna or rna probe hybridises only to its complementary sequence so clones bearing the mutated gene stay dark on the autoradiograph, and elisa reads antigen-antibody interactions to flag either pathogen antigens or the antibodies raised against them.
concepts.key_idea: Amplify, hybridise, or bind -- pcr finds the trace nucleic acid, probes find the exact sequence, elisa finds the protein signature.
concepts.textbook_ref: lebo110.txt lines 250-282 (early diagnosis, PCR for low pathogen loads and mutations, radiolabelled probe, ELISA principle)
question_patterns: how can pcr detect a pathogen before disease symptoms appear
what is a probe and how does it locate a mutated gene
why does a clone carrying the mutated gene fail to show on the autoradiograph
on what principle does elisa work for infection detection
name the molecular techniques used for early diagnosis of disease
how is pcr used in suspected aids and cancer patients

solution_steps.explain: Pathogen numbers only grow large once symptoms exist; pcr multiplies even minute bacterial or viral nucleic acid loads to detectable levels -- standard for hiv screening and for spotting gene mutations in suspected cancers.
A single-stranded dna or rna probe tagged with a radioactive molecule binds its complementary sequence in a cell clone; autoradiography exposes the match.
A clone carrying the mutated gene stays off the photographic film because the probe lacks complementarity with the altered sequence.
Elisa rests on antigen-antibody interaction -- detecting either pathogen antigens (proteins, glycoproteins) or the antibodies the patient has made against the invader.

concepts.title: Transgenic Animals and Their Five Uses
concepts.definition: Transgenic animals carry dna manipulated to possess and express an extra foreign gene -- rats, rabbits, pigs, sheep, cows and fish exist but over 95 percent are mice -- serving to study gene regulation and normal physiology, to model human diseases such as cancer, cystic fibrosis, rheumatoid arthritis and alzheimer's, to manufacture biological products (alpha-1-antitrypsin for emphysema; rosie the cow's human alpha-lactalbumin milk at 2.4 grams per litre), to test vaccine safety such as polio, and to speed chemical toxicity testing.
concepts.key_idea: Sensitivity is the design goal -- transgenic testers react to toxins faster and model human diseases that ordinary animals cannot.
concepts.textbook_ref: lebo110.txt lines 283-334 (definition, five purposes, Rosie 1997, polio vaccine testing, toxicity testing)
question_patterns: what makes an animal transgenic and why are most transgenic animals mice
list the purposes for which transgenic animals are produced
how do transgenic animals serve as models of human disease
what did the transgenic cow rosie produce and how much per litre
how are transgenic mice used in testing the safety of the polio vaccine
why do transgenic animals speed up chemical toxicity testing

solution_steps.explain: Transgenic animals have their dna manipulated to hold and express a foreign gene; mice make up over 95 percent of all such animals.

They reveal how genes are regulated and affect development (insulin-like growth factor work), and they model human diseases -- cancer, cystic fibrosis, rheumatoid arthritis, alzheimer's -- letting new treatments be tried.

Engineered to carry product genes, they make human alpha-1-antitrypsin for emphysema and similar candidates for pku and cystic fibrosis; rosie's 1997 milk carried human alpha-lactalbumin at 2.4 g/l, better balanced for babies.
Transgenic mice stand in for monkeys in polio vaccine safety testing, and animals made extra sensitive to toxic substances deliver chemical safety results sooner.

concepts.title: Ethical Issues: GEAC, Patents and Biopiracy
concepts.definition: Manipulating living organisms demands regulation because released gene-modified organisms can have unpredictable ecological effects -- india's answer is the genetic engineering approval committee (geac), which decides the validity of gm research and the safety of public introductions; disputes over patenting life and the biopiracy of traditional resources -- the 1997 basmati patent on an indian farmer variety, claims over turmeric and neem -- drive countries to legal shields such as the amended indian patents bill.
concepts.key_idea: Biodiversity-rich but cash-poor nations hold the raw materials and the knowledge -- biopiracy is the uncompensated extraction of both.
concepts.textbook_ref: lebo110.txt lines 335-402 (GEAC, patent anger, Basmati 1997, turmeric and neem, biopiracy definition, Indian Patents Bill)
question_patterns: why is regulation needed for genetically modified organisms
which indian body approves gm research and what does it decide
define biopiracy and give an indian example
how was basmati rice patented by a foreign company and why was it contested
what complaints surround patents on turmeric and neem based products
how does the amended indian patents bill respond to exploitation of bio resources

solution_steps.explain: Modifying organisms cannot continue unregulated -- moral standards must weigh benefits and harms, and ecological introductions of gene-modified organisms carry unpredictable results.
India's geac (genetic engineering approval committee) rules on the validity of gm research and the safety of releasing gm organisms for public services.

Companies patent products built on genetic material and knowledge that farmers and indigenous communities developed over centuries; in 1997 an american company patented a 'new' basmati derived from indian farmer varieties, restricting others' sales.

Biopiracy is the unauthorised, uncompensated use of bio-resources by multinationals; with industrialised nations rich in money but poor in biodiversity, india countered through turmeric and neem challenges and the second amendment of the indian patents bill.

worked_examples.source_ref: lebo110.txt lines 127-137 (Bt protoxin activation; exercise 4, lines 417-466)
worked_examples.question_pattern: Crystals of bt toxin made by bacillus thuringiensis do not harm the bacterium itself. Pick the correct reason and explain the chemistry.

solution_template.explain: The bacteria are not resistant, the toxin is not immature, and no special sac encloses it -- the real reason lies in the toxin's chemical state.
The toxin exists as an inactive protoxin; only an insect's alkaline gut solubilises the crystals and converts it to the active form, so the bacterium itself is never exposed to active toxin.
Once activated in the insect midgut, the toxin binds epithelial cells and forms pores that swell and lyse them, killing the larva.

worked_examples.source_ref: lebo110.txt lines 74-79 (meristem virus freedom; exercise 1, line 408-410)
worked_examples.question_pattern: A banana stock is infected with a virus. Which plant part should be cultured to raise healthy plants, and why does that part stay clean?

solution_template.explain: The apical or axillary meristem is the part best suited for regenerating virus-free plants.
Even in a systemically infected plant, the meristem remains free of virus, so excising and growing it in vitro yields disease-free banana (likewise sugarcane and potato).

worked_examples.question_pattern: The transgenic cow {cow_name} produced milk enriched with a human protein. Identify the protein, its concentration, and why the milk mattered for babies.

solution_template.explain: Rosie, the first transgenic cow (1997), secreted human alpha-lactalbumin in her milk at 2.4 grams per litre.
Human-protein-enriched milk is a more balanced food for human babies than ordinary cow milk -- proof that transgenic animals can manufacture medicinal biological products.
